basis: Existing owner-authored portfolio scope, repository artifacts and individually reviewed Figma exports. Design intent is not a measured outcome.

projects.title: Orkest HQ
projects.category: Enterprise SaaS · CRM and shared workspace patterns
projects.summary: Helping a CRM user find the right lead, add what is missing and move the record forward.
context: Orkest combines CRM, sales, inventory and finance in one workspace. I worked on its navigation, record lists and forms. The challenge was to make a large product feel familiar without making every module work in exactly the same way.

I focused this story on leads. Someone needs to find the right record, understand who owns it and decide whether it is ready to become a contact and an opportunity. That sequence gave the CRM screens a practical order.
constraints: Several business modules share the same workspace.
Lists need enough detail to compare records without overwhelming the next action.
Creating, editing and converting a lead have different responsibilities.

decisions.heading: Find the lead that needs attention
body: All leads, My leads and Unassigned answer a simple question: whose work am I looking at? I kept those views close to search and Filters, while the rows carry qualification details. Ownership and readiness remain separate, so an unassigned lead does not disappear inside a score.

The filter screens show the next part of the task: choose criteria, see what needs correcting and check the result. Showing these states together makes the list easier to understand than a single polished table.
decisions.leadIn: First, the list has to explain whose work is visible.
decisions.tradeoff: The list needs enough information to choose a record; the detail view can carry the explanation behind it.

decisions.heading: Make creating and editing feel connected
body: The create-lead form groups contact information and qualification. A side panel explains what follows, including that the score is calculated after saving. The form can collect the input without pretending an unsaved lead already has a settled result.

Editing uses the same record structure, with guidance about saving and duplicate checks. For handoff, I would keep the open rules beside these screens: which fields are required, who can assign an owner and what stays filled in if saving fails.
decisions.leadIn: Once a lead needs to be added, the interface changes from comparison to careful entry.
decisions.tradeoff: A shorter form is useful only if it still collects what the next person needs.

decisions.heading: Explain what conversion will do
body: The detail panel brings the lead information back together before conversion. Its explanation says that conversion creates a contact and an opportunity while keeping the lead history. That gives the action a meaning beyond its button label.
I used the same approach across the workspace: keep location, record identity and action priority familiar, then let each module add the detail its task needs.
decisions.leadIn: Saving is an intermediate step. The next design problem is moving the record forward without losing its context.
decisions.tradeoff: Shared patterns should save people from relearning the interface without forcing every business task into the same form.

projects.delivery: The design work connects the module directory, lead list, filter states, capture form, edit form and conversion detail. Together, they show how the record moves through the CRM.
projects.outcome: The screens give the team a concrete sequence to build and review. I do not have measured task-time or adoption results for this work.

journey.question: How can one workspace support different business jobs without making people relearn the interface at every module?
journey.opening: I started with the list because that is where the next task becomes visible. The form and detail view then carry the same lead forward, with more information as the decision becomes more specific.
steps: Find the lead that needs attention
Make creating and editing feel connected
Explain what conversion will do
journey.reflection: A useful shared system starts with repeated tasks. In this case, ownership, record identity and the next action were more useful foundations than a collection of matching cards.

evaluation: Find an unassigned lead, apply a filter and switch ownership views. Can the person explain which records are now included?
Follow a failed save into retry and conversion. Check that ownership, input and record history survive each transition.
projects.scopeNote: Original CRM design screens with sample data. These explain my design contribution; server validation, permissions and cross-module synchronization require implementation testing.

projects.title: piHub
projects.category: Fintech · Creditor, investor and administrator journeys
projects.summary: Making a financial application easier to follow when several people have a part in the decision.
context: piHub connects creditors, investors and administrators. Each person sees a different part of the same process: one submits an application, another reviews an offer or request, and an administrator manages access and records.
I worked on forms, information hierarchy and status language across these roles. The central problem was helping someone understand what had happened, what was still needed and who should act next.
constraints: Creditor, investor and administrator roles need different information.
Waiting for another person is a legitimate part of the process.
A review decision needs the relevant request and its supporting detail.

decisions.heading: Show what has been submitted
body: The creditor sequence starts with company information, acknowledges an application and brings submitted work into a list. The acknowledgement says that the application was received; it should not be confused with approval.
In the list, written statuses sit beside the information needed to compare applications. A person can see which requests are waiting and which have moved forward without opening every record.
decisions.leadIn: The creditor’s first need is an overview of what has already been submitted.
decisions.tradeoff: A compact list helps comparison, but a request that needs attention also needs a specific explanation.

decisions.heading: Give investors their own view of the work
body: Investors enter the process with different questions. They need to define an offer, review products and inspect incoming credit requests. Their screens therefore give those objects more attention than the creditor profile.
I kept the relationship between the roles in the status language. A label such as Awaiting Approval needs one agreed meaning even when each role sees a different page.
decisions.leadIn: That view is only one side of the process. Investor priorities require a different object and information hierarchy.
decisions.tradeoff: The roles can share components and status names while giving different actions priority.

decisions.heading: Put the request beside the review decision
body: The administrator views add the other side of the handoff. A request list leads into company details, and a credit-review page collects the information and attachments needed to consider the request. Approve and Disapprove sit with the record they affect.

Access denial is a separate situation. Its recovery screen gives a way back, while permission checks still belong to the application and server. I would review these boundaries with the team before treating the cross-role flow as complete.
decisions.leadIn: The journey also needs a boundary: some actions or records are not available to the current account.
decisions.tradeoff: Review actions need enough context to support a decision; showing more financial fields alone does not make the decision clearer.

projects.delivery: The creditor, investor and administrator designs show the application from different responsibilities. The additional review screens make the handoff visible within this case.
projects.outcome: The design establishes a role-based structure and a shared way to discuss state changes. Live processing, uploads and synchronized notifications remain engineering work.

journey.question: How does a financial workflow remain understandable when the next step belongs to another person?
journey.opening: I followed the application across the roles. The screens need to share a meaning for each status, while giving creditors, investors and administrators different information and actions.
steps: Show what has been submitted
Give investors their own view of the work
Put the request beside the review decision
journey.reflection: Waiting is easier to understand when the interface explains the dependency. Sometimes the right next step belongs to another person.

evaluation: Ask a creditor to identify who owns the next step after submission and what would require a response.
Trace an application returned for changes across creditor, investor and administrator views; check that their status language describes the same event.
projects.scopeNote: Original role prototypes with owner-confirmed sample financial and contact data. Separate screens do not establish working financial processing or permission enforcement.

projects.title: Yarsha
projects.category: Mobile · Web3 messaging and wallet context
projects.summary: Connecting conversations and wallet actions without losing track of the person on the other side.
context: Yarsha brings contacts, chats, groups and wallet-related actions into one mobile app. I worked on how people move between those parts, from finding a contact to looking back at a transaction.
The challenge was the change in attention. Starting a conversation is a familiar action. Choosing a recipient and an asset needs a more careful check, even when it begins in the same app.
constraints: Names and wallet identifiers both help distinguish contacts.
Tokens and NFTs need different selection details.
Groups introduce membership and administrator responsibilities.

decisions.heading: Find the right person
decisions.leadIn: Before any conversation or transfer, the person needs confidence that they have found the right contact.
body: The contacts list pairs a display name with a shortened wallet identifier. Names help recognition; the identifier helps distinguish people with similar names or avatars.

When search finds no contact, the query stays visible and the screen offers ways to continue. The empty state belongs to the search journey, so it needs to help someone decide whether to change the query, add a contact or invite someone.
decisions.tradeoff: A short identifier keeps the list readable, but the full address needs to be available when it matters.

decisions.heading: Keep the conversation and its history together
decisions.leadIn: After recognition, the product can shift from finding someone to understanding the relationship.
body: The conversation keeps the contact in the header and the composer at the bottom. From there, the profile gives more context through the address, shared media, groups and links.
In-thread search keeps the conversation visible and adds a match count with previous and next controls. Someone looking for an old link can stay in the place where it was shared.
decisions.tradeoff: The profile can hold extra detail without asking people to leave the chat for every small check.

decisions.heading: Choose the recipient before the asset
decisions.leadIn: The familiar social context now gives way to a decision that needs greater precision.
body: Send Money starts with a person or wallet-address search. Token and NFT selection follow as separate decisions, with names and symbols for tokens and artwork for NFT collections.
That sequence leaves room to check who receives the asset before deciding what to send. A later authorization step still needs to bring the recipient, network, asset and amount together.
decisions.tradeoff: Distinct steps give each decision attention, while the previous choices need to stay easy to inspect and change.

decisions.heading: Make group membership understandable
decisions.leadIn: A relationship can expand from one person into a shared space with its own responsibilities.
body: Creating a group begins with choosing members. The group details then bring its identity, description and shared content together. Editing keeps the name, description, administrator and member settings in one place.

The administrator screen makes the owner visible and gives adding an administrator its own action. Invitation has a separate screen for copying or sharing the link. These are different responsibilities, so I kept them easy to tell apart.
decisions.tradeoff: Compact group settings are convenient, but ownership and permission changes deserve clear labels.

decisions.heading: Leave a useful record of the transaction
decisions.leadIn: The story ends with a detail view someone can return to and question.
body: The transaction-detail view separates spent and received assets from the destination and fee. It gives someone a place to inspect the event after leaving the conversation.

The source frame also contains a Blastscan label in this Solana-oriented design. That is an unresolved detail to check with engineering: the network and explorer destination must agree before the link can be trusted.
decisions.tradeoff: A concise result is useful when it also gives access to the details behind it.

projects.delivery: The complete screens cover contacts, chat, search, asset selection, group management and transaction detail. The two additional group screens show how membership and responsibility are managed after creation.
projects.outcome: The design connects the social and financial parts of the app. I have no verified adoption or transaction-performance measurements to report.

journey.question: How can a familiar conversation become the starting point for Web3 actions without making every action feel equally casual?
journey.opening: I organized the walkthrough around a person: find them, open the conversation, choose an action and keep enough context to check what happened afterward.
steps: Find the right person
Keep the conversation and its history together
Choose the recipient before the asset
Make group membership understandable
Leave a useful record of the transaction
journey.reflection: Keeping a person in view helps a complicated journey feel connected. The interface also needs to slow down enough when the action becomes consequential.

evaluation: Ask someone to detect an incorrect recipient, asset or network before authorizing a transfer.
Exercise rejection, a delayed confirmation and returning from an explorer. Check whether retrying could accidentally duplicate the action.
projects.scopeNote: Complete original mobile designs with sample data. Wallet authorization, network behavior and transaction outcomes are outside what these static screens can verify.

projects.title: Zapp Today
projects.category: Mobile logistics · Customer, driver and operations
projects.summary: Helping customers describe a delivery, review the request and understand the handoff to a driver.
context: A delivery involves several people with different jobs. The customer describes what needs moving, the driver handles the next stop, and operations needs enough context to resolve an exception.
My contribution covered these connected mobile journeys. I focused this case on how the customer request becomes a clear delivery task, while keeping customer and driver screens distinct.
constraints: Customers and drivers act on the same delivery with different priorities.
Pickup, parcel and service choices need to stay connected through review.
Address lookup, routing and payment depend on real services.

decisions.heading: Make the first choice clear
body: The account-entry screen gives Create account and Sign in their own explanation. New customers have a clear starting point, and returning customers can go straight to the route they need.
Registration and code verification continue that path. Keeping the mobile number and resend action understandable is part of making the next step feel connected to the previous one.
decisions.leadIn: Before the delivery request, account entry needs to make the two starting paths understandable.
decisions.tradeoff: Giving the new-customer action more emphasis should not make sign-in hard to find.

decisions.heading: Build the request one decision at a time
body: Pickup entry offers address search, a landmark route and current location. The parcel screen then asks what is being carried, with named package types and a description field. Service selection follows after that context exists.

The review screen brings the request together before payment: pickup, recipient, parcel, vehicle and a sample estimate. An edit-recipient action gives the customer a way to correct a detail without starting again.
decisions.leadIn: After entry, the question becomes what the service needs to know about the item.
decisions.tradeoff: Breaking up the request keeps each step focused, while the final review needs to show how the choices fit together.

decisions.heading: Give the driver a clear next stop
body: The driver view distinguishes a confirmed pickup from the next drop-off. Progress and the current stop take priority, with a separate route for reporting a stop issue.
This is where the handoff needs an agreed rule. The team has to define which driver action changes the delivery status and what the customer or operations team sees afterward.
decisions.leadIn: The viewpoint now changes from preparing a request to carrying out a stop.
decisions.tradeoff: Driver and customer views need a shared account of progress, even though their next actions differ.

decisions.heading: Separate a finished delivery from payment records
body: The completion screen names the handoff and offers a return to availability. Settlement and earnings depend on verified server records, so they remain a different responsibility.

For implementation review, I would check an interrupted handoff, a repeated completion action and the return to the driver dashboard. Those situations are part of making the completion message dependable.
decisions.leadIn: The final moment is not simply a success graphic: it must explain which responsibility has ended.
decisions.tradeoff: A reassuring completion message must describe what is actually known to be finished.

projects.delivery: The screenshots connect entry, pickup, parcel and service choices, review, the driver’s next stop and completion. The added pickup and review screens fill in the customer journey between the earlier examples.
projects.outcome: The design gives the customer and driver different priorities within one delivery story. Routing, dispatch, payment and delivery performance still need real-service evidence.
related: Review the full journey before redesigning

journey.question: How can the same delivery feel clear to the person booking it and the person carrying it out?
journey.opening: The customer journey moves from account entry to pickup, parcel details, service selection and a final review. The driver then needs an operational view of the same delivery.
steps: Make the first choice clear
Build the request one decision at a time
Give the driver a clear next stop
Separate a finished delivery from payment records
journey.reflection: A delivery flow becomes easier to explain when every screen answers a practical question: what are we moving, where is it going, what happens next and who acts now?

evaluation: Compare the customer milestone with the driver action for pickup, arrival and completion; each pair should describe the same service event.
Walk through an intermediate-stop failure and delayed completion update. Check that the next action remains clear without implying settlement has occurred.

publicReference.note: Current public website, checked 5 November 2026. Its presentation may differ from the customer-app design contribution described in this case.

projects.scopeNote: Customer iOS and driver prototype references are labeled as design work. Map content and prices are illustrative; current lookup, dispatch, tracking and payment are not certified. Historical project year remains unverified.

projects.title: Morajaa
projects.category: B2B consulting · Service and sector website
projects.role: UX, content structure and website design contribution
projects.summary: Helping a prospective client understand a consulting service before starting a conversation.
context: Morajaa presents consulting services across several sectors. A visitor may know the business problem they face without knowing which service name fits it. I worked on information architecture, service and sector pages, and the path to an inquiry.
The challenge was to explain enough of the engagement for a useful first conversation, while keeping a long service page easy to scan.
constraints: Visitors may recognize a business problem before a service category.
Long service explanations still need a useful first scan.
Service and sector pages should connect without repeating the same introduction.

decisions.heading: Explain the work before asking for contact
body: The market-entry page moves from a service introduction into setup, ongoing support and a named process. Those sections give the inquiry action some context.
I wanted a first scan to answer whether the service fits, with enough detail underneath for someone who is ready to read further. The homepage gives that explanation a place in the wider offer.
decisions.leadIn: The opening needs to earn attention by making the service recognizable.
decisions.tradeoff: Short introductions help people get started, but an involved engagement also needs room for detail.

decisions.heading: Make the process easy to follow
body: Named stages help a visitor understand the shape of an engagement before reading every paragraph. The service examples use that structure for different kinds of work, including joint ventures, tender management and HR outsourcing.
The reusable pattern is the reading order. Each page still needs its own explanation of what the work includes and where the consultancy’s responsibility ends.
decisions.leadIn: Once relevance is established, the visitor needs a more concrete picture of the work.
decisions.tradeoff: A shared page pattern should make services easier to compare without making them sound interchangeable.

decisions.heading: Offer a second route through the sectors
body: Some visitors begin with a service. Others begin with their industry. Sector pages give healthcare and technology visitors a more familiar starting point, then lead into relevant service detail.
I treated these as connected paths through the same offer. The sector page should help someone find the right explanation without making them read the same introduction again.
decisions.leadIn: A visitor may arrive by service or by sector, so the page must reconnect those paths.
decisions.tradeoff: Two entry routes are useful when they lead into a coherent set of pages.

projects.delivery: The work includes homepage, service and sector structures, with complete design screens showing how the reading paths connect.
projects.outcome: The design gives the consultancy room to explain a complex engagement. Inquiry or sales performance was not measured for this case.

journey.question: How can a visitor evaluate a complex consulting engagement before speaking to sales?
journey.opening: The homepage introduces the offer. Service pages explain the work in more detail, and sector pages give visitors another way to find what is relevant to their business.
steps: Explain the work before asking for contact
Make the process easy to follow
Offer a second route through the sectors
journey.reflection: People often arrive with their own description of a problem. A service website should help them connect that description to the work on offer.

evaluation: Ask a prospective client to identify the relevant engagement stage and explain what the consultancy would deliver.
Check whether the process section answers the question raised by the service promise before the visitor reaches contact.
projects.scopeNote: Historical website designs from the primary file. Sample business and regulatory copy is not independent verification of services, legal claims or client outcomes.

projects.title: Masteriyo
projects.role: Product UI and UX contribution within a team
projects.summary: Helping course authors move from a blank course to lessons, quizzes and question details.
context: Masteriyo is an established WordPress LMS. I contributed product UI and UX within its wider team, including course and quiz flows and reusable interaction patterns.

A course author moves through several levels of detail: the course, its sections, individual lessons, a quiz and its answers. The challenge was keeping that structure understandable as the editing work became more detailed.
constraints: The work sits within an established WordPress LMS and product team.
Sections, lessons, quizzes and answers are different levels of content.
Shared patterns need room for each question type’s settings.

decisions.heading: Help an author start a course
body: A title and description give the course an identity. The empty builder then offers concrete ways to add content, including a section, assignment or quiz, with documentation close by.
That is more useful than an empty panel, although the equal weight of the creation actions leaves a question for review: does a new author know which unit to create first?
decisions.leadIn: An empty course is the first authoring task, not a dead end.
decisions.tradeoff: Offering several starting points gives flexibility; the most useful first action still needs to be clear.

decisions.heading: Keep the outline visible as content grows
body: The populated builder places lessons inside their section. Add New Content belongs to the group, while Add New Section sits outside it. The layout helps explain what belongs where.

Section and lesson editors then open the detail for the selected item. Row actions keep editing, duplication and deletion close to that item, while the surrounding outline gives the author a place to return.
decisions.leadIn: Once content exists, the interface must explain how it belongs together.
decisions.tradeoff: Compact actions save space, but they need clear names, keyboard access and safe deletion behavior.

decisions.heading: Break quiz setup into manageable steps
body: Quiz setup separates Info, Questions and Settings. The author names the quiz before moving into the denser work of writing and configuring its questions.
Next and Cancel also need clear consequences. The handoff should explain what is saved, what is validated and what happens to unfinished work when someone leaves.
decisions.leadIn: A quiz adds a different configuration task inside that course structure.
decisions.tradeoff: Staging the setup reduces competing decisions, provided the author can still tell where their work is saved.

decisions.heading: Keep the question in its quiz context
body: The editor keeps the question list above the expanded question. Type and points have a separate place from the answer rows, with settings below. An author can work on an answer without losing track of which question is open.

The true-or-false and multiple-choice screens show where the pattern stays familiar and where the content changes. Correct-answer feedback also needs more than color, and reordering needs an alternative to dragging.
decisions.leadIn: Question editing is the deepest level shown here, where configuration density grows quickly.
decisions.tradeoff: A consistent editor helps authors learn the pattern, while each question type still needs enough room for its own settings.

projects.delivery: The eight complete authoring designs cover course details, the empty builder, outline, section and lesson editing, quiz setup and two question configurations. They are presented as team work within my contribution.
projects.outcome: The design separates course organization from assessment detail. I do not have learner-completion, adoption or task-time measurements for this work.

journey.question: How do you help a course author build something complex without making every configuration decision compete at once?
journey.opening: The walkthrough starts with the first course information, grows into a course outline and then moves into quiz configuration. The interface keeps the larger structure in view as the author works on a smaller part.
steps: Help an author start a course
Keep the outline visible as content grows
Break quiz setup into manageable steps
Keep the question in its quiz context
journey.reflection: A course builder is easier to follow when it keeps answering which level the author is editing. Course structure and answer configuration need different amounts of attention.

evaluation: Ask a course author to create a section, add a lesson and configure a quiz without losing their place in the course outline.
Review question reordering, an invalid answer and cancellation with unsaved changes; verify keyboard access and feedback alongside the visual hierarchy.
artifacts: Explore the original Masteriyo design file
projects.scopeNote: Historical product-team design work, not sole authorship of Masteriyo. Static screens do not certify saving, scoring or learner outcomes.

projects.title: Mokshya.io
projects.role: Website UX and product communication contribution
projects.summary: Introducing an AI/Web3 lab and giving visitors a clear way to explore its work or start a project.
context: I worked on website UX and product communication for Mokshya. The retained homepage introduces an AI-Native Web3 R&D lab, with a broad headline followed by a more specific explanation of its work.
The website needed to serve visitors at different stages. Some want to understand the lab and its experiments; others already have a project to discuss.
constraints: Technical positioning needs a concrete supporting explanation.
Exploring the work and starting an inquiry are different visitor intentions.
Navigation and visual identity must support the opening message.

decisions.heading: Give the headline a concrete explanation
body: The headline sets the direction, while the supporting sentence names AI agents, applications and Web3 infrastructure. That second layer does the practical work of explaining what the lab is talking about.
I treated the headline and description as a pair. The visual opening can attract attention, but the next sentence needs to help someone explain the offer in their own words.
decisions.leadIn: Begin with the actual words and hierarchy visible in the retained design.
decisions.tradeoff: A broad introduction needs a specific follow-up before it can support a useful decision.

decisions.heading: Separate exploring from starting a project
body: Explore and Start a project meet different intentions. The navigation also makes Experiments visible, giving someone who is still evaluating the lab a place to look further.
The distinction matters because a visitor should be able to learn before committing to an inquiry. A project-ready visitor should also have a direct route forward.
decisions.leadIn: Once the proposition is visible, the visitor needs a next step that matches their intent.
decisions.tradeoff: Two actions are useful when their labels make the difference between them clear.

decisions.heading: Let the presentation support the explanation
body: The dark opening and colored glow give the page a recognizable look. The compact navigation and logo row sit around the introduction without taking over the headline.
For the next review, I would inspect the actual destinations and narrow-screen layout. The retained desktop image gives a useful view of the composition, but those behaviors need the working site.
decisions.leadIn: The presentation can invite confidence without becoming the evidence for a technical claim.
decisions.tradeoff: Visual polish can introduce a technical business; specific work and accurate relationship labels have to support its claims.

projects.delivery: The retained homepage shows the opening, navigation and two main actions within my website communication contribution.
projects.outcome: The case explains the visible website decisions. No conversion, comprehension or technical-delivery result is available to report.

journey.question: How can an AI/Web3 lab introduce its work and offer a useful next step without asking visitors to trust an unsupported claim?
journey.opening: I focused on the opening sequence: introduce the lab, explain the offer in more concrete terms and give each visitor a useful next step.
steps: Give the headline a concrete explanation
Separate exploring from starting a project
Let the presentation support the explanation
journey.reflection: The next sentence after a broad promise often matters more than another visual flourish. It gives the visitor something concrete to understand.

evaluation: Ask a first-time visitor to explain the lab’s offer from the category label, headline and supporting sentence, then identify the next route they would choose.
Inspect the actual Explore, Experiments and Start a project destinations when a working source is available; check the evidence behind each capability and relationship claim.

projects.title: Designerex
projects.role: Design contribution within a broader marketplace
projects.summary: Giving fashion-rental browsing enough practical detail to help someone compare garments.
context: My contribution to Designerex focused on browsing and listing patterns within the wider marketplace. Garment photography attracts attention, while size, availability and rental information help someone decide whether an item fits their plans.
The design challenge was the relationship between those two jobs. The catalogue needs room for the clothes without making practical information hard to find.
constraints: Garment photographs vary in proportion and visual weight.
Comparable rental details need consistent placement.
Subtle navigation and filters still need clear interaction feedback.

decisions.heading: Let the photograph introduce the garment
body: The image is the natural starting point in a fashion catalogue. Keeping practical details in a consistent area beneath it lets the photograph stay prominent while the renter begins to compare.
A card cannot carry every rental condition. I focused the browsing pattern on the information someone needs to decide whether an item is worth opening.
decisions.leadIn: The first job of the listing is to invite a closer look.
decisions.tradeoff: Too much metadata overwhelms the photographs; too little makes every comparison require another page.

decisions.heading: Keep comparable details in predictable places
body: A renter should not have to search a different part of each card for the same kind of information. Stable placement and labels make repeated listings useful as a comparison tool.

The detail page can then carry the fuller explanation. I would review the pattern with long garment names, different image proportions and unavailable options, since those are where a neat catalogue can become hard to use.
decisions.leadIn: Interest is not enough to choose a rental; comparable details become the priority.
decisions.tradeoff: Consistency helps scanning, while the detail view gives each listing the room it needs.

decisions.heading: Preserve the browsing context
body: Filters and navigation should help someone work through the catalogue and return to the place they left. The quiet visual treatment can support that work without hiding the controls.
Keyboard focus, active-filter feedback and the route back from a listing would be part of my next review. A premium-looking grid still needs predictable behavior.
decisions.leadIn: As the person moves into detail and back, interaction must protect the work they have already done.
decisions.tradeoff: Subtle controls need enough contrast and feedback to remain easy to use.

projects.delivery: This case describes my contribution to browsing and listing design. The dated homepage and catalogue captures show the current public marketplace as supporting context.
projects.outcome: The design work concerns image-led discovery and practical comparison. I do not claim ownership of the whole marketplace or measured booking improvements.
related: When polish hides a decision problem

journey.question: How can fashion discovery stay expressive while making rental decisions dependable?
journey.opening: I organized the story around the move from noticing a garment to comparing it. The repeated card pattern carries the essentials, while deeper detail supports a closer decision.
steps: Let the photograph introduce the garment
Keep comparable details in predictable places
Preserve the browsing context
journey.reflection: The photograph starts the interest. A dependable listing pattern helps someone decide whether that interest fits their actual plans.

evaluation: Ask a renter to compare two garments for occasion, size, price and availability without relying on memory.
Review a long garment name, an unavailable date and a missing photograph to check whether the rental decision remains understandable.

projects.title: Splashnode
projects.category: Technical platform · Website design and frontend
projects.summary: Explaining a technical platform through the work a prospective buyer needs to do.
context: I worked on website design and frontend implementation for Splashnode. The existing project material describes content, device and data-management capabilities. The website needed to make those capabilities understandable to a prospective buyer.
The challenge was explaining where the platform fits before asking someone to work through a long feature list.
constraints: Technical capabilities need a recognizable use case.
Introductory content and deeper detail have different jobs.
The frontend must preserve hierarchy as copy and viewport size change.

decisions.heading: Connect a capability to a task
body: A feature name becomes more useful when someone can connect it to work they recognize. I organized the explanation around the use case before adding the supporting capability detail.
That gives the opening a different job from the deeper sections. The introduction establishes relevance; the rest of the page helps someone evaluate the fit.
decisions.leadIn: Begin with the buyer’s task rather than a wall of feature names.
decisions.tradeoff: Short explanations help a first scan, while technical buyers still need access to meaningful detail.

decisions.heading: Keep the next step easy to find
body: A visitor may want more detail, an example or a conversation. I treated action placement as part of the reading order, so the next step follows the information that makes it useful.
The page should make it possible to keep evaluating the offer without repeatedly interrupting the reader with the same inquiry request.
decisions.leadIn: Once the capability is relevant, the visitor needs a way to investigate further.
decisions.tradeoff: Calls to action need enough visibility without competing with every explanation.

decisions.heading: Work through the layout in code
body: Frontend work let me review the composition with real text lengths, wrapping and navigation behavior. Those constraints help reveal whether a section still makes sense outside the initial design frame.
I kept the visual hierarchy and reusable page patterns connected to that implementation work. The retained preview shows the website’s visual context.
decisions.leadIn: The reading sequence then has to work outside the ideal desktop artboard.
decisions.tradeoff: Reusable sections need to tolerate content changes, not just match the first arrangement.

projects.delivery: The contribution joins website information hierarchy, responsive composition and frontend structure.
projects.outcome: This case describes the website work. Operational reliability and commercial outcomes of the underlying platform are outside the evidence available here.

journey.question: How can a technical platform website help a buyer connect capabilities to a real use case?
journey.opening: I connected capability explanations to a reading path: understand the use case, inspect the relevant detail and find a sensible next step.
steps: Connect a capability to a task
Keep the next step easy to find
Work through the layout in code
journey.reflection: Working with the content in the browser makes hierarchy a practical design decision. The page has to explain the offer after the ideal text lengths change.

evaluation: Ask a buyer to connect one platform capability to a task in their own work, then find an appropriate evaluation step.
Review the page with real copy lengths and narrow viewports; check that the use-case explanation still leads naturally into capability detail.
projects.scopeNote: Historical owner-retained website preview. Original capture date and current platform capability are not independently verified.

projects.title: Grid Labs
projects.summary: Making hosting plans easier to compare without turning the page into a wall of specifications.
context: Grid Labs is a hosting and infrastructure website. I worked on its commercial hierarchy, plan presentation, domain-search affordance and static frontend.
A prospective customer needs to understand which service fits and how plans differ. The challenge was putting those decisions ahead of the full specification list.
constraints: Plan attributes need consistent labels, units and billing periods.
Stacked cards make direct comparison harder on narrow screens.
A static site must be clear about what its actions actually provide.

decisions.heading: Keep plan differences in a stable order
body: Equivalent plan details need the same labels, order and units. That lets someone compare the differences instead of remembering where each attribute appeared on the previous card.

Technical detail still has a place, but the attributes that change the choice deserve more attention. Current prices and commercial terms belong with the service owner; the historical site is used here to discuss the pattern.
decisions.leadIn: Start by making equivalent plan attributes genuinely comparable.
decisions.tradeoff: Giving every specification equal weight makes the information harder to compare.

decisions.heading: Help comparison survive a narrow layout
body: Stacking cards preserves their content, but it makes comparison depend more on memory. Repeated attribute labels help someone connect the same detail across plans.
I would review a narrow layout with two plans that differ in one important way. If finding that difference depends on remembering an offscreen card, the comparison needs more support.
decisions.leadIn: That structure faces its hardest test when the plans no longer fit side by side.
decisions.tradeoff: A layout can fit the screen while still making the decision harder.

decisions.heading: Make the next step honest
body: The domain-search field suggests a useful task, but the website in this case is a static implementation. Its destination and response need to match that scope.
The same applies to purchase actions. The page can help someone understand a plan without implying that account creation, billing and provisioning are all part of the demonstrated work.
decisions.leadIn: Choosing a plan then leads beyond the limits of the static website.
decisions.tradeoff: An attractive action needs a clear destination and an accurate promise.

projects.delivery: A commercial website and static frontend, with the focus on service hierarchy, plan comparison and maintainable page structure.
projects.outcome: The work makes the plan-comparison decisions visible. It does not establish a live hosting-management, billing or provisioning service.

journey.question: How can a hosting buyer compare plans without carrying every specification in memory?
journey.opening: I focused the page on choosing a service, comparing its plans and understanding what happens after the next action.
steps: Keep plan differences in a stable order
Help comparison survive a narrow layout
Make the next step honest
journey.reflection: The label and unit beside a number are part of the comparison. Consistent detail often helps more than another highlighted specification.

evaluation: Ask a buyer to choose between adjacent plans and explain which specification drove that choice.
Repeat the comparison on a narrow screen with longer plan labels; preserve units and distinctions without requiring horizontal page scrolling.
artifacts: Explore the Grid Labs hosting website
projects.scopeNote: Historical design material and a dated public static-site reference. Offers may be out of date; domain lookup, billing and provisioning were not verified.

projects.title: Hamro Idea
projects.category: Software studio · Brand, website and frontend
projects.summary: Helping a software studio explain its services and give prospective clients a useful route to contact.
context: Hamro Idea needed a website that could explain a software studio’s offer. I worked across positioning, information architecture, responsive UI and frontend implementation.
I began with what a prospective client needs to understand: whether the studio can help, what the work involves and which example makes that promise believable.
constraints: Client vocabulary may differ from internal service names.
Repeated page patterns need distinct service explanations.
Layouts must tolerate real copy lengths and image proportions.

decisions.heading: Explain the service in the client’s terms
body: The homepage introduces the offer, and the services page gives it more detail. I organized that explanation around the problem a service addresses and the work it includes.
Keeping those questions close helps a prospective client choose a relevant path without having to understand the studio’s internal vocabulary first.
decisions.leadIn: The prospect first needs to recognize a service that fits the problem.
decisions.tradeoff: Shared sections make the website coherent, while each service still needs its own explanation.

decisions.heading: Put the work near the promise
body: The project index supports a quick scan. A project-detail page then gives one example room for explanation, and About introduces the studio behind it.
I treated those pages as different parts of the evaluation. The sample imagery and business copy in the historical designs show the intended placement of proof, not verified company results.
decisions.leadIn: A relevant service creates a reasonable demand for evidence.
decisions.tradeoff: A project gallery helps discovery; a useful detail page has to explain the contribution.

decisions.heading: Give interested readers somewhere to go deeper
decisions.leadIn: A visitor may want to understand the studio’s thinking before starting a project conversation.
body: The article index offers a short preview before asking someone to open a longer page. The article layout then needs a comfortable reading hierarchy and a route to related material.
This gives someone who is still learning about the studio another useful path before contacting it. The article text in these historical designs is demonstration content.
decisions.tradeoff: Editorial content earns its place when it helps a visitor evaluate the offer.

decisions.heading: Make starting a conversation straightforward
body: The contact page keeps the first request small with name, email and message. Navigation and the surrounding identity remain familiar after the visitor leaves the service or project pages.
The implementation still needs persistent labels, appropriate field semantics and clear validation, progress and success states. Those details let the simple layout work as a usable form.
decisions.leadIn: After understanding the offer and inspecting relevant work, the prospect needs a clear route to a conversation.
decisions.tradeoff: A short form reduces the first commitment, while good labels and feedback make that commitment understandable.

projects.delivery: The work connects service pages, project examples, About, articles and contact within a reusable multi-page frontend.
projects.outcome: The case shows how design and code support the evaluation path. Search rankings and inquiry growth are not measured outcomes of this work.
related: Working with a designer in Nepal

journey.question: How can a software studio make its offer understandable and give a prospect a reason to believe it?
journey.opening: The journey moves from the service offer into relevant work and, when someone is ready, a direct inquiry. About and article pages give visitors another way to learn more.
steps: Explain the service in the client’s terms
Put the work near the promise
Give interested readers somewhere to go deeper
Make starting a conversation straightforward
journey.reflection: Designing and building the pages together helped me treat content variation as part of the layout, not something to fix after delivery.

evaluation: Ask a prospect to choose a relevant service, locate supporting work and reach contact with enough context to describe their need.
Review the form using keyboard input, invalid email, submission failure and success; check persistent labels and meaningful feedback.

publicReference.label: Explore the current Hamro Idea demo
publicReference.note: Public demo, checked 5 November 2026. This current implementation is a separate reference from earlier studio work.

projects.scopeNote: Historical Figma designs contain sample copy and imagery; the current public demo is a separate dated reference. Company claims and form delivery are not certified by the designs.

projects.title: Zakra Furniture
projects.category: WordPress and Elementor · Furniture starter site
projects.role: Storefront UI and template design contribution
projects.summary: Designing a furniture starter site that can still work after the demo content changes.
context: A furniture starter site serves both a shopper and the person maintaining the catalogue. I contributed storefront hierarchy, reusable sections, product cards, typography and spacing for the WordPress/Elementor context.
The challenge was keeping an image-led catalogue coherent when photographs, product names and the amount of content vary.
constraints: Furniture photography varies in crop and aspect ratio.
Product names and catalogue size change after the demo is delivered.
Site owners need editing freedom with clear spacing and type rules.

decisions.heading: Give product photographs room to vary
body: Furniture images differ in proportions and visual weight. A repeatable image area helps the catalogue read as one collection, but its crop rule needs care.

A fixed crop can create a neat rhythm while hiding part of a product. Containing the whole image preserves the object but can leave uneven space. I would choose the rule against varied product photography, not only the ideal demo images.
decisions.leadIn: The first source of variation is the photography itself.
decisions.tradeoff: The most even grid is not always the clearest view of the product.

decisions.heading: Keep each product card easy to read
body: Product names and decision details need predictable positions. A longer name or a missing optional detail should not make a card feel like a different component.
For the reusable template, I would check wrapping, missing images, different product counts and narrow layouts. Those are normal content conditions for a site owner.
decisions.leadIn: A stable image treatment still leaves the rest of the product card to handle change.
decisions.tradeoff: A stable card pattern needs room for ordinary variation.

decisions.heading: Make editing part of the design
body: A site owner needs to know which sections can be repeated, removed or rearranged. Simple spacing and type rules help preserve the page while leaving useful editing freedom.
That is why I describe the contribution as a starter-site interface and its content behavior. The initial storefront is one example of how the template can be used.
decisions.leadIn: Those repeated cards belong to sections a site owner needs to edit over time.
decisions.tradeoff: Too much freedom can produce visual drift; overly rigid sections make routine editing harder.

projects.delivery: A reusable storefront interface and CMS-aware content patterns, shown with the official published starter-site reference.
projects.outcome: The case explains catalogue and template decisions. Checkout, stock accuracy, fulfillment and sales performance were not verified.

journey.question: How can a furniture starter site remain coherent after a site owner replaces the demo content?
journey.opening: I treated the storefront as a reusable pattern. The demonstration needs to look good, and the rules need to survive ordinary catalogue editing.
steps: Give product photographs room to vary
Keep each product card easy to read
Make editing part of the design
journey.reflection: A useful template has to survive its second set of content. Long names and varied photographs belong in the design review from the start.

evaluation: Replace demo content with long product names, inconsistent photograph proportions and missing descriptions; check that the catalogue hierarchy survives.
Ask a site owner to edit a category and product card, then inspect the result on a narrow screen without manually repairing the layout.
projects.scopeNote: Official Zakra Furniture reference with upstream attribution. My contribution is the scoped storefront/template work, not ownership of Zakra or a complete ecommerce backend.

projects.title: Neverwinter Live Parser
projects.summary: Helping a player understand an encounter summary without losing the context behind its numbers.
context: Neverwinter Live Parser is a personal tooling project with a Windows-oriented Electron app and a React renderer. I worked on the information model, summary hierarchy and implementation-aware interface.
The challenge is what a total means. A player needs to know which encounter, actor, time range and filters produced the number before drawing a conclusion from it.
constraints: A total depends on its encounter, actor, time range and grouping.
Malformed or incomplete events limit what can be inferred.
Dense data needs a readable overview and a route into detail.

decisions.heading: Keep the encounter attached to the number
body: One renderer fixture gives a player 999 total damage across the available data, but only 120 within the selected encounter. The expected row uses 120 and derives 12 DPS for the ten-second encounter. These are test-fixture values.

That example makes the interface requirement clear: the selected encounter changes the meaning of the summary. The screen should keep that context available instead of silently substituting a broader total.
decisions.leadIn: A number first needs enough context to be interpreted.
decisions.tradeoff: A compact total needs a clear scope.

decisions.heading: Let the overview lead into a specific question
body: Raw-line parsing, encounter aggregation and renderer rows have different responsibilities in the source. An event’s applied amount, the way events are grouped and the row a player reads are related decisions.

The tests distinguish applied damage from base magnitude and cover grouping player-owned summons and companions. An overview needs enough context for someone to understand those groupings before investigating further.
decisions.leadIn: With the context established, the overview should lead into a specific question.
decisions.tradeoff: The summary should stay readable while keeping its underlying assumptions inspectable.

decisions.heading: Make incomplete data visible
body: A malformed-line test expects an issue result and an unknown event type. Other fixtures distinguish placeholder encounters from meaningful combat totals.
Those cases give uncertainty a concrete place in the model. The app still needs execution with representative logs to establish how completely these conditions are handled and communicated.
decisions.leadIn: That investigation must also reveal when the source data cannot support an answer.
decisions.tradeoff: A precise-looking number should not conceal that the input is incomplete.

code.label: Malformed-input contract from the actual parser test, excerpt

projects.delivery: The public repository exposes parser, aggregation and view-model fixtures. The browser setup reference shows how the tool introduces its log dependency.
projects.outcome: The design and source explain how encounter context should stay connected to the summary. The Windows app and parser accuracy were not independently executed in this portfolio review.

journey.question: How can a combat summary make complex events readable without hiding the assumptions behind its numbers?
journey.opening: I organized the story from the summary back to its supporting data. The public source provides concrete examples of the rules behind that relationship.
steps: Keep the encounter attached to the number
Let the overview lead into a specific question
Make incomplete data visible
journey.reflection: The useful summary is the one a player can question. Keeping its context nearby makes a number easier to interpret.

artifacts: Inspect real parser cases and malformed-input expectations
Inspect encounter-scoped rows and ownership grouping
Read the Electron application and runtime manifest
evaluation: Trace one displayed metric back to known combat events and the documented calculation rule.
Use empty, malformed and interrupted log fixtures before evaluating parsing correctness, session recovery or speed.
projects.scopeNote: Personal project, separate from ownership of Neverwinter. Public browser view is an idle setup state; fixture values are examples, not player results or live telemetry.

projects.title: SassBoilerplate
projects.category: Archived frontend learning · Sass and build workflow
projects.summary: Learning how a small Sass codebase connects to a build workflow.
context: SassBoilerplate is an earlier learning archive based on JR Cologne’s Gulp Starter Kit. My contribution was learning and adaptation around that starter, with its original author and MIT license retained.
The source offers a simple way to explain what I was working through: where styles begin, how imports connect and what the build tasks do with them.
constraints: The original starter-kit authorship and MIT attribution must remain clear.
The archive has a small actual import structure.
Historical dependencies need review before use with a current runtime.

decisions.heading: Start at the stylesheet entry point
decisions.leadIn: The entry point gives the first concrete place to inspect the workflow.
body: The archived app.sass imports _includes, which imports base/_base. That gives the styles a short dependency path that is easy to inspect.

Source comments explain that empty helper, module, partial and global placeholders were removed. The remaining structure is small, so there is no need to describe a larger component or token architecture that is not there.
decisions.tradeoff: Folders are useful when they have a responsibility, not simply because a starter can include them.

code.label: Actual entry and shared import, excerpted from the learning archive

decisions.heading: Understand what each build task owns
decisions.leadIn: After locating the Sass source, the next question is how it becomes browser output.
body: The Sass task reads Sass and SCSS, handles compilation and errors, adds prefixes, minifies the result and writes source maps. Other tasks handle templates, JavaScript, images and copied dependencies.
Reading those responsibilities helped connect source organization with the output. It also shows why a modern migration has to check the historical toolchain as well as the stylesheet files.
decisions.tradeoff: Separate tasks make the workflow easier to follow, while older dependencies can still limit whether it runs today.

decisions.heading: Keep the learning archive in context
decisions.leadIn: The last decision is how to present and reuse the work responsibly.
body: The README credits JR Cologne and the upstream kit, with the MIT license. It also records historical tooling requirements that need review before any current use.
I include the archive to explain the learning and adaptation. It is not a new framework or a maintained package release.
decisions.tradeoff: An archive can explain how the work developed without presenting old tooling as a current recommendation.

projects.delivery: A public learning archive with inspectable Sass imports, named build tasks and upstream attribution.
projects.outcome: The source explains the relationship between stylesheet organization and build responsibilities. The historical dependencies were not installed or executed for this case.

journey.question: What did a small starter workflow teach me about making frontend structure understandable?
journey.opening: The walkthrough follows the files from the Sass entry point to the generated output. It stays with the structure that is actually present in the archive.
steps: Start at the stylesheet entry point
Understand what each build task owns
Keep the learning archive in context
journey.reflection: A small working dependency path is easier to maintain than a large folder structure with no clear responsibilities.

artifacts: Read the archive status and upstream attribution
Inspect the actual named build tasks
evaluation: Ask a developer unfamiliar with the archive to locate the source styles, build entry point and generated output.
Review upstream attribution and dependency age before deciding what can be learned from the structure or reused in a maintained project.
projects.scopeNote: Historical adaptation of JR Cologne’s MIT-licensed starter kit. Upstream authorship is retained; the archive is not a new framework or a current dependency recommendation.
